questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 2 month history of breathlessness and dry cough. She has never smoked. Urine dipstick shows non-visible haematuria. Chest X-ray (see item resources) shows multiple large, round, well-defined opacities throughout both lungs.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple round, well-defined 'cannonball' opacities in both lungs.

questions.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
questions.e: Multiple large round 'cannonball' metastases are classically from renal cell carcinoma, supported here by haematuria.

steps.x: **Cannonball** lung metastases + **haematuria** = renal cell carcinoma.

elim: Breast spreads to lung, but cannonball lesions with haematuria point to the kidney.
Colorectal cancer spreads first to the liver.
A primary lung cancer is usually a single mass, not many round lesions.
She is a woman; prostate spreads to bone.

steps.x: **E. Renal cell carcinoma.** Cannonball metastases: classically renal cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with breast cancer treated 5 years ago has 6 weeks of aching bone pain that is worse at night. She has lost 3 kg. Her adjusted calcium is 2.71 mmol/L and ALP is raised. An isotope bone scan is arranged to look for bone metastases.
questions.q: Which site is most likely to show metastases on the bone scan?
questions.e: Bone is the most common site of metastasis overall, and the spine is the most common site of bone metastases, causing night pain and raised calcium.

steps.x: Night bone pain + high calcium after breast cancer = bone metastases, most often in the **spine**.

elim: The proximal femur is often involved, but less commonly than the spine.
Metastases distal to the elbow and knee are rare.
Ribs are affected, but less often than the vertebrae.
The skull is a less common site.

steps.x: **E. Spine.** Bone is the commonest site of metastasis; the spine is the commonest bony site.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman had breast cancer treated with mastectomy 3 years ago. She has a 6 week history of breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. She has no fever. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. CT chest shows multiple rounded nodules of varying size in both lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Breast cancer commonly spreads to lung, liver and brain; new breathlessness and cough with multiple nodules after breast cancer is lung metastasis.

clues: breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough
multiple rounded nodules of varying size
steps.x: Cancer history + new **breathlessness and cough** + **multiple nodules** = lung metastases.

elim: She has no fever, and pneumonia gives consolidation, not multiple nodules.
PE gives sudden symptoms and filling defects, not lung nodules.
Pneumonitis occurs within months of radiotherapy and gives patchy shadowing in the field.
Sarcoid gives bilateral hilar nodes in younger adults.

steps.x: **B. Lung metastases.** Lung metastases present with breathlessness and cough.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man had a sigmoid colectomy for adenocarcinoma 2 years ago. He has 2 months of fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort and 7 kg weight loss. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. His ALP and GGT are raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
questions.e: The liver is the most common site of colorectal metastasis; liver metastases cause hard irregular hepatomegaly, abnormal LFTs and weight loss.

steps.x: Colorectal cancer + RUQ pain + weight loss + abnormal LFTs = **liver metastases**: a hard, knobbly liver.

elim: Caput medusae is portal hypertension from cirrhosis.
Murphy's sign is acute cholecystitis, with fever.
A pulsatile mass is an aortic aneurysm.
Liver metastases enlarge the liver, not the spleen.

steps.x: **B. Hard, irregular hepatomegaly.** Colorectal cancer spreads to the liver first (portal venous drainage).

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She has never had a seizure before. She had breast cancer treated 2 years ago. She has had mild headaches for 3 weeks. She now has mild weakness of her left hand. Her glucose is 5.6 mmol/L and sodium is 139 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A first seizure with headache and a focal deficit in a patient with breast cancer is brain metastasis until proven otherwise.

steps.x: First seizure + **focal sign** + **cancer history** = brain metastases.

elim: Her glucose is normal.
Her sodium is normal.
A first seizure at 52 with a focal deficit and cancer history needs a structural cause.
Syncope does not cause a focal weakness or headaches.

steps.x: **A. Brain metastases.** Brain metastases: headache, seizures, focal neurological deficit.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man had a melanoma excised from his back 4 years ago. He has a 2 month history of night sweats, fevers, tiredness and 8 kg weight loss. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. He has firm, non-tender left axillary lymph nodes and a smooth enlarged liver.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: B symptoms, nodes and hepatomegaly in a patient with a previous cancer mean metastasis until proven otherwise.

clues: melanoma excised from his back 4 years ago
night sweats, fevers, tiredness and 8 kg weight loss
steps.x: Known primary + **B symptoms** + nodes draining the primary site + liver = metastatic spread.

elim: CFS does not cause weight loss, fevers, nodes or hepatomegaly.
Depression does not cause fevers, nodes or an enlarged liver.
Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss but not nodes or hepatomegaly.
TB is possible but the node site and cancer history point to metastasis.

steps.x: **D. Metastatic melanoma.** A new symptom in a patient with a cancer history is metastasis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has 3 months of pain in his hips and lower back. He has not seen a doctor for years. X-rays of the pelvis and lumbar spine show multiple dense, white, sclerotic lesions. His ALP is 640 U/L and calcium is 2.38 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
questions.e: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men to spread to bone and classically causes sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions with a high ALP.

steps.x: Older man + **sclerotic (osteoblastic)** bone lesions + high ALP = **prostate**.

elim: Renal cell carcinoma gives lytic, not sclerotic, bone lesions.
Lung cancer usually gives lytic deposits.
Myeloma gives punched-out lytic lesions with a normal ALP.
Thyroid metastases are lytic.

steps.x: **D. Prostate.** Prostate: osteoblastic bone metastases. Most others: lytic.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a 3 week history of constant mid-thoracic back pain. It is worse lying flat and wakes her at night. Her legs have normal power, tone and sensation. Her temperature is 36.7°C. She has no history of osteoporosis or trauma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New back pain in a cancer patient, especially thoracic, at night or lying flat, is a spinal metastasis until proven otherwise.

clues: worse lying flat and wakes her at night
steps.x: **New back pain** + **cancer** + night/lying flat pain = spinal metastasis.

elim: AS starts in young adults with morning stiffness that improves with exercise.
Discitis is usually febrile, often after a procedure or bacteraemia.
Mechanical pain improves with rest, not worse lying flat at night.
Osteoporotic fractures are sudden and she has no osteoporosis or trauma.

steps.x: **E. Spinal metastasis.** The spine is the commonest site of bone metastasis; new back pain in cancer = urgent MRI.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with breast cancer has 1 week of thirst, constipation and confusion. She has new pain in her ribs and pelvis. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised calcium?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH, a raised ALP and new bone pain in breast cancer is from bone metastases releasing calcium by osteolysis.

clues: new pain in her ribs and pelvis
steps.x: High calcium with **low PTH** = malignancy. New **bone pain** + high ALP = **bone metastases**.

elim: She has no history of high calcium or antacid intake, and has bone pain.
PTH is suppressed, not raised.
Sarcoid does not cause new bone pain with a raised ALP in cancer.
Her vitamin D is normal.

steps.x: **A. Bone metastases.** Raised calcium suggests bone involvement in metastatic disease.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man had prostate cancer treated 4 years ago. He has a 4 week history of low back pain that is present at rest and at night. He has no leg weakness, numbness or bladder symptoms. His temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Focal tenderness over a lumbar spinous process
Reduced lumbar flexion with sacroiliac tenderness
questions.e: Spinal metastases cause focal bone tenderness over the affected vertebra; neurological deficits appear later with cord compression.

clues: no leg weakness, numbness or bladder symptoms
steps.x: Cancer + **night/rest pain** + no neurology = bone metastasis causing **focal bony tenderness**.

elim: He has no leg weakness, so there is no cord compression yet.
This suggests a disc prolapse with nerve root irritation.
This fits ankylosing spondylitis in a younger man.
He has no numbness or bladder symptoms.

steps.x: **B. Focal tenderness over a lumbar spinous process.** Examination in metastatic disease: bone tenderness, hepatomegaly, neurological deficit.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has 2 months of pain in her right hip and lower back. She has never smoked. X-ray shows several lytic lesions in her pelvis and lumbar spine. Serum protein electrophoresis shows no paraprotein. Her thyroid and renal ultrasound are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the primary tumour?
questions.e: In women, bone metastases most often come from breast cancer (lung in smokers); myeloma, thyroid and kidney have been excluded here.

steps.x: Woman + bone metastases + non-smoker + myeloma, thyroid and kidney excluded = **breast**.

elim: Cervical cancer spreads locally to the pelvis, rarely to bone.
Colon cancer spreads first to the liver.
Endometrial cancer rarely spreads to bone.
Ovarian cancer spreads transcoelomically to the peritoneum.

steps.x: **A. Breast.** Bone metastases: prostate (men), breast (women), lung.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has 3 months of change in bowel habit to looser stools and 6 kg weight loss. He is anaemic. CT shows multiple low-density lesions throughout the liver but none in the lungs or bones. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the primary tumour?
questions.e: Liver-only metastases with change in bowel habit and iron deficiency anaemia point to colorectal cancer, which reaches the liver first via the portal vein.

clues: multiple low-density lesions throughout the liver
steps.x: **Change in bowel habit** + **iron deficiency** + liver deposits = colorectal primary.

elim: Lung cancer favours brain, bone and adrenals and does not change bowel habit.
Oesophageal cancer causes dysphagia, not looser stools.
Prostate spreads to bone, not the liver alone.
Thyroid cancer spreads to lung and bone.

steps.x: **A. Colorectum.** Most common colorectal metastasis site: the liver.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had a nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma 3 years ago. He has 6 weeks of increasing breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss. His temperature is 36.9°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: Renal cell carcinoma classically spreads to the lungs as multiple round cannonball metastases, causing breathlessness.

steps.x: Renal cell carcinoma + new breathlessness = **cannonball** metastases.

elim: Bilateral hilar nodes are typical of sarcoidosis.
Pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure.
Consolidation is pneumonia, with fever.
Upper lobe fibrosis follows TB or sarcoidosis.

steps.x: **D. Multiple round, well-defined opacities.** Renal cell carcinoma: cannonball lung metastases.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman had breast cancer treated 6 years ago and was discharged from follow-up. For 2 months she has had a deep ache in her left hip that is now waking her at night. Her GP initially thought it was osteoarthritis. She has lost 3 kg. Her hip movements are full but painful.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New night bone pain with weight loss in a patient with past breast cancer is a bone metastasis until proven otherwise, even years later.

steps.x: Past cancer + new **night bone pain** + weight loss = bone metastasis, however long ago.

elim: This gives lateral hip pain on lying on that side, without weight loss.
Osteoarthritis is worse with use, eases with rest and limits movement.
There was no fall and she can still move the hip fully.
PMR gives bilateral girdle pain and stiffness, not one-sided night pain.

steps.x: **A. Bone metastasis.** New symptom + cancer history = metastasis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with lung cancer has a 1 week history of headache that is worse in the morning, with vomiting. He is drowsy but rousable. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 164/92 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: New headache and vomiting with papilloedema in a cancer patient suggests brain metastases with raised ICP, needing urgent imaging; MRI is used for suspected CNS involvement.

clues: worse in the morning, with vomiting
steps.x: Cancer + morning headache + vomiting + **papilloedema** (+ falling pulse, rising BP) = raised ICP: **urgent brain imaging**.

elim: An EEG does not show a mass or raised ICP.
LP with raised ICP and a possible mass risks coning.
Raised ICP needs urgent same-day assessment.
Skull X-ray cannot show brain metastases.

steps.x: **E. Urgent MRI brain.** Suspected brain metastases: urgent MRI; never LP first.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 3 months of pain in his left upper arm and 6 kg weight loss. He has no known cancer. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the left humerus. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no obvious primary and no other lesions. Serum protein electrophoresis is normal.
questions.q: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis and its origin?
o: Image-guided biopsy of the bone lesion
questions.e: Imaging plus biopsy is the gold standard: histology of the lesion confirms metastasis and its tumour of origin.

clues: lytic lesion in the left humerus
steps.x: Imaging has found the lesion; only **tissue** tells you what it is and **where it came from**.

elim: A bone scan shows other deposits but cannot say what they are.
PET-CT may find a primary but does not give tissue.
Waiting delays diagnosis and treatment.
Tumour markers are not specific enough to confirm the origin.

steps.x: **A. Image-guided biopsy of the bone lesion.** Gold standard for metastatic disease: imaging plus biopsy.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has just been diagnosed with a 4 cm grade 3 breast cancer with palpable axillary nodes. She mentions recent fatigue and weight loss, and her ALP is raised. The breast team wants to know whether the cancer has spread before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line staging investigation?
questions.e: First-line staging for metastatic spread is CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

steps.x: Looking for spread **everywhere** at once = **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**.

elim: Ultrasound only looks at the abdomen and misses lungs and bones.
A chest X-ray misses small deposits and the abdomen.
MRI liver images one organ only.
This does not look for distant spread.

steps.x: **C. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.** First-line staging: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with prostate cancer has new aching pain in his ribs. He is otherwise well. His GP sends a full blood count and LFTs and wants one more blood test that would most suggest his cancer has spread to bone.
questions.q: Which blood test is most useful?
questions.e: Bloods in metastatic disease include FBC, LFTs and calcium; a raised calcium suggests bone involvement.

clues: new aching pain in his ribs
steps.x: Bone breakdown releases calcium: **raised calcium** suggests bone involvement.

elim: Amylase reflects the pancreas, not bone.
CRP is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
Ferritin reflects iron stores and inflammation.
TSH does not reflect bone involvement.

steps.x: **A. Adjusted serum calcium.** Bloods: FBC, LFTs, calcium (raised calcium = bone involvement).

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of new thoracic back pain. A plain X-ray of the thoracic spine shows no abnormality. His leg power and sensation are normal. His temperature is 36.8°C. His pain is getting worse at night.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: New back pain in a cancer patient needs MRI spine first-line; plain X-rays miss early metastases.

steps.x: New back pain + cancer = **MRI spine**, even when the X-ray is normal.

elim: CT abdomen does not image the spinal cord or marrow well.
A bone scan does not show the cord or soft tissue extension.
PSA shows disease activity but not where it is.
A normal X-ray does not exclude metastasis; waiting risks cord compression.

steps.x: **C. MRI whole spine.** New back pain in cancer: MRI spine first-line.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman had a right hemicolectomy for colon cancer 18 months ago. She now has 6 weeks of fatigue and a dull ache under her right ribs. She is not jaundiced. She drinks no alcohol. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern on her liver function tests?
o: Normal LFTs with low albumin only
Raised ALP and GGT with normal bilirubin
questions.e: Liver metastases cause hepatomegaly and abnormal LFTs, typically a raised ALP and GGT from infiltration while bilirubin is normal until late.

clues: dull ache under her right ribs
steps.x: Colorectal cancer + RUQ ache = liver deposits, which give an **infiltrative** pattern: **ALP and GGT** up.

elim: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is Gilbert's or haemolysis.
Liver deposits usually raise ALP and GGT.
ALT in the thousands is acute hepatitis or ischaemia.
This pattern suggests alcohol, and she does not drink.

steps.x: **C. Raised ALP and GGT with normal bilirubin.** Liver metastases: hepatomegaly, abnormal LFTs (raised ALP/GGT), weight loss.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma has three brain metastases on MRI with surrounding oedema. She had headache and vomiting, which have improved after starting dexamethasone. She is independent and her extracranial disease is stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for her brain metastases?
o: Craniotomy to remove all three lesions
Observation with repeat MRI in 6 months
questions.e: Brain metastases are treated with steroids to reduce oedema together with radiotherapy.

steps.x: Steroids have treated the oedema; the tumours themselves need **radiotherapy**.

elim: Surgery is for a single accessible lesion, not three.
Mannitol is a short-term rescue for herniation, not treatment.
She has not had seizures, and it does not treat the tumour.
Untreated metastases will progress.

steps.x: **E. Radiotherapy.** Brain metastases: steroids plus radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has newly diagnosed colon cancer with three metastases in the liver on CT. He is fit, works full time and has no other illnesses. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. He asks what happens next.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Discussion at the oncology multidisciplinary team meeting
questions.e: Metastatic disease is managed with systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy) planned by the MDT and oncology team.

steps.x: Metastatic + fit = **active treatment**, which is planned by the **MDT**.

elim: Metastatic cancer in a fit man needs active treatment planning.
He is fit and well; end-of-life care is not appropriate yet.
Waiting allows progression without treatment.
Removing the primary alone ignores the liver disease.

steps.x: **B. Discussion at the oncology multidisciplinary team meeting.** Metastatic disease: systemic therapy through the oncology MDT.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has severe pain in her left thigh on walking. X-ray shows a mixed lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric femur. Her Mirels score is 10. She has a life expectancy of more than 6 months and is fit for an anaesthetic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the femoral lesion?
questions.e: A Mirels score of 9 or more (or a lytic lesion involving over 50% of cortex with weight-bearing pain) is an indication for prophylactic orthopaedic fixation.

clues: severe pain in her left thigh on walking
steps.x: **Mirels 9 or more** = fix it before it breaks.

elim: Bisphosphonates reduce skeletal events but will not prevent this imminent fracture.
A Mirels score of 10 means a high fracture risk.
Radiotherapy helps pain but does not stabilise a bone at high fracture risk.
Bed rest does not reduce fracture risk and causes harm.

steps.x: **C. Prophylactic internal fixation.** Prophylactic fixation: Mirels ≥9 or >50% cortical involvement with weight-bearing pain.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with breast cancer has multiple lytic bone metastases in her spine and pelvis. Her pain is controlled with regular analgesia. Her adjusted calcium is 2.58 mmol/L and creatinine is normal. Her dental check is up to date. The oncologist wants to reduce her risk of fractures.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional long-term treatment?
questions.e: Bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid inhibit osteoclasts and are used long-term for bone metastases to reduce fractures and pain.

clues: dental check is up to date
steps.x: Bone metastases + fracture prevention = **bisphosphonate** (check teeth and kidneys first).

elim: Supplements do not stop tumour-driven osteolysis.
Loop diuretics do not protect bone.
Steroids worsen bone loss.
Thiazides raise calcium and do not protect bone.

steps.x: **D. IV zoledronic acid.** Bone metastases: bisphosphonates long-term.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman has metastatic breast cancer in her liver and bones. She has declined further chemotherapy. She has pain in her back and hips, feels sick, and wants to remain at home with her daughter. She is spending most of the day in bed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Referral to the community palliative care team
questions.e: In advanced metastatic disease, palliative care with symptom control is most important, here delivered at home as she wishes.

clues: pain in her back and hips
most of the day in bed
steps.x: Declined treatment + symptoms + **wants to stay at home** = community **palliative care**.

elim: She has declined chemotherapy.
Major surgery is not appropriate in a bed-bound patient focused on comfort.
More scans will not change her care plan.
Radical treatment does not fit her goals; any palliative radiotherapy would be planned with palliative care.

steps.x: **D. Referral to the community palliative care team.** Palliative care (symptom control) is the most important management in many cases.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with metastatic melanoma phones his GP. For 3 days he has had a new headache that is worst on waking, and he has vomited twice this morning. He has never had headaches before. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral codeine and review in 1 week
questions.e: New headache and vomiting in a cancer patient suggests brain metastases with raised ICP and needs urgent same-day assessment.

steps.x: New morning headache + **vomiting** + cancer = possible raised ICP: an emergency, not a GP review.

elim: Analgesia delays assessment of possible raised ICP.
A routine appointment is weeks away and too slow.
A new headache in a cancer patient should not be labelled migraine.
Waiting risks deterioration from raised intracranial pressure.

steps.x: **D. Same-day hospital assessment.** New headache and vomiting in cancer: urgent assessment for brain metastases.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has a 2.5 cm breast carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. Sentinel node biopsy shows tumour deposits in two left axillary lymph nodes. CT shows no other spread.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route by which the tumour reached the axilla?
questions.e: Breast cancer commonly spreads by lymphatics to the regional axillary nodes, entering lymphatic vessels and surviving in the lymph.

steps.x: Tumour in the **regional draining nodes** = **lymphatic** spread, typical of breast cancer.

elim: Canalicular spread is along ducts or airways, such as bile ducts or bronchi.
The nodes are separate from the tumour, not invaded by continuity.
Blood-borne spread goes to lung, liver, brain and bone, not regional nodes first.
Transcoelomic spread is across body cavities, such as ovarian cancer to peritoneum.

steps.x: **D. Lymphatic spread.** Routes: haematogenous (commonest), lymphatic (breast), transcoelomic (ovary), canalicular.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a squamous cell carcinoma of the right lung. Six months after diagnosis he develops seizures, and MRI shows two enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction in the brain. He has no lymph node involvement in the neck.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route by which the tumour reached his brain?
questions.e: Haematogenous spread is the most common route and carries lung cancer cells to highly vascular organs such as the brain, where they lodge at the grey-white junction.

clues: two enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction
steps.x: Deposits at the **grey-white junction**, where small vessels narrow = **blood-borne** spread.

elim: Canalicular spread is along ducts, airways or subarachnoid space, not deposits in brain tissue.
The lung is far from the brain; this is not spread by continuity.
Lymphatics carry tumour to nodes, not into the brain.
Transcoelomic spread crosses body cavities such as the peritoneum.

steps.x: **C. Haematogenous spread.** Haematogenous spread is commonest and favours lung, liver, brain and bone.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how colon cancer cells form liver metastases. Tumour cells are seen trapped in liver sinusoids after travelling in the portal blood. Only some of them go on to form secondary tumours in the liver tissue.
questions.q: Which step must occur next for a trapped tumour cell to form a liver deposit?
o: Epithelial invasion of the bowel wall
Lymphatic drainage to the mesenteric nodes
questions.e: After arresting at a distant site, tumour cells must extravasate out of the vessel and then proliferate to form a secondary tumour.

clues: Only some of them go on to form secondary tumours
steps.x: Already **in the blood** and **arrested** in the liver: next they must **leave the vessel** (extravasate), then grow.

elim: Local invasion happened at the primary site, at the start.
Intravasation is entering the blood, which has already happened.
This is a different route, not the next step in the liver.
Shedding onto serosal surfaces is transcoelomic spread.

steps.x: **B. Extravasation through the vessel wall.** Metastatic cascade: invade, intravasate, survive, arrest, extravasate, proliferate.

questions.stem: A pathologist examines a resected bowel carcinoma. Tumour cells have broken through the basement membrane into the submucosa, and some are seen inside the lumen of small veins in the bowel wall. The patient later develops liver metastases.
questions.q: Which process do the tumour cells inside the veins show?
questions.e: Tumour cells first invade local tissue, then enter blood vessels or lymphatics (intravasation) and must survive in the circulation.

clues: inside the lumen of small veins
steps.x: Local **invasion** first, then **entering** the vessel = **intravasation**.

elim: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not spread.
Extravasation is leaving a vessel at the distant site.
Metaplasia is change from one mature cell type to another.
This is spread across a body cavity, not into veins.

steps.x: **C. Intravasation.** Intravasation = entering vessels; extravasation = leaving them at the distant site.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with renal cell carcinoma has severe pain in his right upper arm. X-ray shows a well-defined destructive lesion with thinning of the humeral cortex. He is at risk of fracture. His adjusted calcium is 2.82 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the bone lesion?
o: Loss of blood supply to bone
questions.e: Most cancers other than prostate, including renal, cause osteolytic lesions via osteoclast activation, weakening bone and risking fracture.

clues: destructive lesion with thinning of the humeral cortex
steps.x: **Destructive (lytic)** lesion from a non-prostate cancer = **osteoclasts** eating the bone.

elim: Defective mineralisation is osteomalacia, with low calcium.
Osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions are typical of prostate cancer.
Osteomyelitis is not caused by renal cell carcinoma.
Avascular necrosis affects the femoral head, not a destructive humeral lesion.

steps.x: **E. Osteoclast activation causing osteolysis.** Prostate: osteoblastic. Lung, renal, thyroid (and often breast): osteolytic.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has abdominal distension and weight loss. CT shows bilateral ovarian masses with many small nodules over the omentum and peritoneum, and ascites. There are no liver or lung metastases and no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the peritoneal nodules?
o: Blood-borne spread via the portal vein
Shedding of tumour cells from the serosal surface
Spread through the systemic arterial circulation
questions.e: In transcoelomic spread, ovarian tumour cells shed from the serosal surface and implant directly onto the peritoneum without needing vascular invasion.

clues: many small nodules over the omentum and peritoneum
steps.x: Peritoneal seeding with **no liver, lung or node** spread = cells **dropping** across the cavity (transcoelomic).

elim: Portal spread gives liver deposits, which she does not have.
Lymphatic spread goes to nodes, and she has none.
That is canalicular spread.
Arterial spread would give lung, brain or bone deposits.

steps.x: **C. Shedding of tumour cells from the serosal surface.** Transcoelomic spread: no vascular invasion needed (ovary, mesothelioma).
